¶
'''Waler''' (wā′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''Wales'' (see def.) + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A horse imported from Australia, particularly from New South Wales. [Anglo-Indian.]

{{smaller block|For sale, a brown ''Waler'' gelding.
{{right|''Madras Mail'', June 25, 1873. (''Yule and Burnell.'')}}
My ''Waler'' was cautiously feeling his way over the loose shale.
{{right|''Rudyard Kipling'', Phantom Rickshaw.}}}}

'''wale-wight†''', ''a.'' [Also ''wall-wight'', ''wa’-wight''; also ''waled wight''; < ''wale''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.'', + ''wight''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.''] Choice and active; chosen and brave.

{{smaller block|<poem>If fifteen hundred ''waled wight'' men
You’ll grant to ride with me.</poem>
{{right|''Auld Maitland'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 220).}}}}

'''Walhalla''', ''n.'' See ''Valhalla''.

'''walie'''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''waly''<sup>1</sup>.

'''walie'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' Same as ''valir''.

'''waling''' (wā′ling), ''n.'' [< ''wale''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.] The weaving of the web of a gabion with more than two rods at a time.

'''walise''' (wa-lēz′), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''valise''.

'''walk''' (wâk), ''v.'' [Under this form are merged two verbs, one strong, the other weak: (''a'') < ME. ''walken'' (pret. ''welk'', pl. ''weolken'', ''welken'', pp. ''walke'', ''iwalken''), < AS. ''wealcan'' (pret. ''weolc'', pp. ''wealcen''), move, roll, turn, revolve, = MD. ''walcken'', cause to move, press, squeeze, strain, D. ''walken'', felt (hats), = OHG. ''walchan'', full (cloth), roll oneself, wallow, MHG. ''walken'' (> It. ''gualcare'', prepare by stamping) = G. ''walken'', full (cloth), felt (hats). (''b'') < ME. ''walkien'' (pret. ''walkede'', ''walkide'', pp. ''walked'') = Icel. ''vālka'', ''volka'', roll, stamp, roll oneself, wallow, = Sw. ''valka'', roll, full (cloth), = Dan. ''valke'', full

{{RunningHeader|Waler|6808|walk}}{{nop}}'''Waler''' (wā′lėr), ''n.''   [< ''Wales'' (see def.) + ''-er''1.]   A horse imported from Australia, particularly from New South Wales. [Anglo-Indian.] {{smaller block|For sale, a brown ''Waler'' gelding. {{right|''Madras Mail'', June 25, 1873. (''Yule and Burnell.'')}}}} {{smaller block|My ''Waler'' was cautiously feeling his way over the loose shale. {{right|''Rudyard Kipling'', Phantom Rickshaw.}}}} '''wale-wight†''', ''a.''   [Also ''wall-wight'', ''wa’-wight''; also ''waled wight''; < ''wale''2, ''a.'', + ''wight''2, ''a.'']   Choice and active; chosen and brave. If fifteen hundred ''waled wight'' men You’ll grant to ride with me. {{smaller block|{{right|''Auld Maitland'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 220).}}}} '''Walhalla''', ''n.'' See ''Valhalla''. '''walie'''1, ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''waly''1. '''walie'''2, ''n.'' Same as ''valir''. '''waling''' (wā′ling), ''n.''   [< ''wale''1 + ''-ing''1.]   The weaving of the web of a gabion with more than two rods at a time. '''walise''' (wa-lēz′), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''valise''. '''walk''' (wâk), ''v.''   [Under this form are merged two verbs, one strong, the other weak: (''a'') < ME. ''walken'' (pret. ''welk'', pl. ''weolken'', ''welken'', pp. ''walke'', ''iwalken''), < AS. ''wealcan'' (pret. ''weolc'', pp. ''wealcen''), move, roll, turn, revolve, = MD. ''walcken'', cause to move, press, squeeze, strain, D. ''walken'', felt (hats), = OHG. ''walchan'', full (cloth), roll oneself, wallow, MHG. ''walken'' (> It. ''gualcare'', prepare by stamping) = G. ''walken'', full (cloth), felt (hats). (''b'') < ME. ''walkien'' (pret. ''walkede'', ''walkide'', pp. ''walked'') = Icel. ''vālka'', ''volka'', roll, stamp, roll oneself, wallow, = Sw. ''valka'', roll, full (cloth), = Dan. ''valke'', full (cloth); prob. akin to L. ''valgus'', bent, ''vergere'', bend, turn, incline: see ''verge''2.]   I. ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To be in action or motion; act; move; go; be current. ȝe ar knyȝt comlokest kyd of your elde, Your worde & your worchip ''walkez'' ay quere [everywhere]. {{smaller block|{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1520.}}}} And ever as she went her toung did ''walke'' In fowle reproch. {{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iv. 5.}}}} '''2.''' To be stirring; be abroad; move about. {{smaller block|Jesus ''walked'' in Galilee; for he would not ''walk'' in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him. {{right|John vii. 1.}}}} She ''walks'' in beauty, like the night Of cloudless climes and starry skies. {{smaller block|{{right|''Byron'', She Walks in Beauty.}}}} '''3.''' To go restlessly about; move about, as an unquiet spirit or specter, or as one in a state of somnambulism. When I am dead, For certain I shall ''walk'' to visit him, If he break promise with me. {{smaller block|{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, ii. 1.}}}} '''4.''' To move off; depart. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|When he comes foorth, he will make theyr cowes and garrans to ''walke''. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} {{smaller block|Browborough has sat for the place now for three Parliaments. . . . I am told that he must ''walk'' if any body would go down who could talk to the colliers every night for a week or so. {{right|''Trollope'', Phineas Redux, i.}}}} '''5.''' To live and act or behave in any particular manner; conduct one’s self; pursue a particular course of life. {{smaller block|Fadres and Modres that ''walken'' in won Schul loue heore children. {{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 143.}}}} {{smaller block|''Walk'' humbly with thy God. {{right|Micah vi. 8.}}}} '''6.''' To move with the gait called a walk. See ''walk'', ''n.'', 5. {{smaller block|O, let me see thee ''walk''; thou dost not halt. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 258.}}}} {{smaller block|He ''walks'', he leaps, he runs — is wing’d with joy. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, i. 443.}}}} '''7.''' To go or travel on foot: often followed by an accusative of distance: as, to ''walk'' five miles. {{smaller block|In his slepe hym thoghte That in a forest faste he ''welk'' to wepe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1235.}}}} {{smaller block|But, look, the morn, in russet mantle clad, ''Walks'' o’er the dew of yon high eastward hill. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 1. 167.}}}} {{smaller block|I was constrained to ''walke'' a foote for the space of seven miles. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 92.}}}} {{smaller block|I’ll ''walk'' aside, And come again anon. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iv. 3.}}}} '''8.''' To move, after a manner somewhat analogous to walking, as an effect of repeated oscillations and twistings produced by expansion and contraction or by the action of winds. Chimneys have been known to move in this manner.—{{smaller|'''The ghost walks.''' See ''ghost''.—'''To walk against time.''' See ''time''1.—'''To walk awry.''' See ''awry''.—'''To walk into,''' to attack. (''a'') To assault; give a beating or drubbing to. (''b'') To fall foul of verbally; give a scolding to. (''c'') To eat heartily of. [Vulgar in all senses.]}} {{smaller block|There is little Jacob, ''walking'', as the popular phrase is, ''into'' a home-made plum-cake, at a most surprising pace. {{right|''Dickens'', Old Curiosity Shop, lxviii.}}}} {{smaller|'''To walk over the course''', in ''sporting'', to go over a course at a walking or slow pace: said of a horse, runner, etc., coming alone to the scratch, and having to go over the course to win; hence, figuratively, to gain an easy victory; attain one’s object without opposition. Also ''to walk over''. Compare ''walk-over''.—'''To walk Spanish.''' See ''Spanish''.—'''To walk tall.''' See ''tall''2.—'''Walk about,''' a military phrase used by British officers to sentinels, to waive the ceremony of being saluted.}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To full, as cloth. {{smaller block|Payment vj d., for the ''walkin'' of ilke eln [ell] of the said xix eln & a half. {{right|''Act. Dom. Conc. A.'' 1488, p. 95. (''Jamieson.'')}}}} '''2.''' To proceed or move through, over, or upon by walking, or as if by walking; traverse at a walk. {{smaller block|If that same demon that hath gull’d thee thus Should with his lion gait ''walk'' the whole world. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 2. 122.}}}} {{smaller block|Yes—she is ours—a home-returning bark; . . . She ''walks'' the waters like a thing of life. {{right|''Byron'', Corsair, i. 3.}}}} '''3.''' To cause to walk; lead, drive, or ride at a walk. {{smaller block|I will rather trust . . . a thief to ''walk'' my ambling gelding. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 319.}}}} {{smaller block|I am much indebted to you For dancing me off my legs, and then for ''walking'' me. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iii. 1.}}}} '''4.''' To escort in a walk; take to walk. {{smaller block|I feel the dew in my great toe; but I would put on a cut shoe, that I might be able to ''walk'' you about; I may be laid up to-morrow. {{right|''Colman and Garrick'', Clandestine Marriage, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|Old Pendennis . . . ''walked'' the new arrivals about the park and gardens, and showed them the carte du pays. {{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, lvi.}}}} '''5.''' To move, as a box or trunk, in a manner having some analogy to walking, partly by a rocking motion, and partly by turning the object on its resting-point in such manner that at each rocking movement an alternate point of support is employed, the last one used being always in advance of the previous one in the direction toward which the object is to be moved.—'''6.''' To send to or keep in a walk. See ''walk'', ''n.'', 8 (''b''). {{smaller block|It is customary to send puppies out at three or four months of age to be kept by cottagers, butchers, small farmers, etc., at a weekly sum for each, which is called ''walking'' them. {{right|''Dogs of Great Brit. and America'', p. 197.}}}} {{smaller block|'''To walk one’s chalks.''' See ''chalk''.—'''To walk the chalk, to walk the chalk-mark,''' to keep straight in morals or manners: a figurative phrase, from the difficulty a drunken man has in walking upon a straight line chalked upon the floor by his comrades to test his degree of sobriety. Compare I., 5.—'''To walk the hospitals,''' to attend the medical and surgical practice of a general hospital, as a student, under one or more of the regular staff of physicians or surgeons attached to such a hospital.—'''Walking the plank.''' See ''plank''.}} '''walk''' (wâk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''walc'', ''walk'', < AS. ''gewealc'', a rolling, moving, = MHG. ''walc'' = Icel. ''válk'', a tossing; from the verb.]   '''1.''' Manner of action; course, as of life; way of living: as, a person’s ''walk'' and conversation. {{smaller block|This is the melancholy ''walk'' he lives in, And chooses ever to increase his sadness. {{right|''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, iv. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Oh for a closer ''walk'' with God! {{right|''Cowper'', Olney Hymns, i.}}}} '''2.''' Range or sphere of action; a department, as of art, science, or literature. {{smaller block|There are strong minds in every ''walk'' of life, that will rise superior to the disadvantages of situation. {{right|''A. Hamilton'', The Federalist, XXXVI.}}}} {{smaller block|She [Mrs. Cibber] made some attempts latterly in comedy, which were not, however, in any degree equal to her excellence in the opposite ''walk''. {{right|''Life of Quin'' (reprint 1887), p. 40.}}}} '''3.''' The act of walking for air or exercise; a stroll: as, a morning ''walk''. {{smaller block|Make an early and long ''walk'' in goodness. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., i. 35.}}}} Nor ''walk'' by moon, Or glittering starlight, without thee is sweet. {{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 655.}}}} To vent thy bosom’s swelling rise In pensive ''walk''. {{smaller block|{{right|''Burns'', The Vision, ii.}}}} '''4.''' Manner of walking; gait; step; carriage. {{smaller block|Catherine . . . watched Miss Thorpe’s progress down the street from the drawing-room window; admired the graceful spirit of her ''walk'', the fashionable air of her figure and dress. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Northanger Abbey, iv.}}}} '''5.''' The slowest gait of land-animals. {{smaller|In the walk of bipeds there is always one foot on the ground; in that of quadrupeds there are always two, and a part of the time three, feet on the ground. When very slow, or with heavy draft-animals when hauling, all four feet touch the ground at once for brief intervals. In the walk of ordinary quadrupeds the limbs move in diagonal pairs, the movement of the pair not being so nearly simultaneous as in}} the trot, and varying much in this respect with the different degrees of speed and with the individual habits of the animal. Compare cut under ''run.'' {{smaller block|Why dost thou not go to church in a galliard and come home in a coranto? My very ''walk'' should be a jig. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 3. 138.}}}} {{smaller block|He stands erect; his slouch becomes a ''walk;'' He steps right onward, martial in his air. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 639.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0612 c3f1.png|center|180px]] {{c|{{smaller|Consecutive Positions of a Horse in Walking.
(After instantaneous photographs by Eadweard Muybridge.)}}}} '''6.''' A piece of ground fit to walk in; a place in which one is accustomed to walk; a haunt. {{smaller block|His ''walk'' The fiery serpent fled and noxious worm. {{right|''Milton'', P. R., i. 311.}}}} {{smaller block|We intend to lay ambushment in the Indian’s ''walks'', to cut off their men. {{right|''N. Thomas'' (Appendix to New England’s Memorial, p. 430).}}}} '''7.''' A place laid out or set apart for walking; an avenue; a promenade. {{smaller block|I saw a very goodly ''walke'' in Mantua roofed over and supported with thirty nine faire pillars. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 148.}}}} {{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') An avenue set with trees or laid out in a grove or wood.}} {{smaller block|Get ye all three into the box-tree; Malvolio’s coming down this ''walk''. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|Up that long ''walk'' of limes I past. {{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lxxxvii.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b''†) ''pl.'' Grounds; a park.}} {{smaller block|He hath left you all his ''walks'', His private arbours and new-planted orchards, On this side Tiber. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 2. 252.}}}} {{smaller block|(''c'') A path in or as in a garden or street; a sidewalk: as, a flagged ''walk;'' a plank ''walk''.}} {{smaller block|He strayed down a ''walk'' edged with box; with apple-trees, pear-trees, and cherry-trees on one side, and a border on the other, full of all sorts of old-fashioned flowers. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xx.}}}} {{smaller block|(''d'') In public parks and the like, a place or way for retirement: as, gentlemen’s ''walk''.}} '''8.''' A piece of ground on which domestic animals feed or have exercise. {{smaller block|He eats the eggs for breakfast and the chickens for dinner, goes in for fancy breeds, and runs up an ornamental ''walk'' for them. {{right|''A. Jessopp'', Arcady, i.}}}} {{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') A tract of some extent where sheep feed; a pasture for sheep; a sheep-walk. See ''sheep-run.''}} {{smaller block|He had ''walk'' for a hundred sheep. {{right|''Latimer'', 1st Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') A place where puppies are kept and trained for sporting purposes.}} {{smaller block|Preference should be given to the home rearing if properly carried out, because it has all the advantages of the ''walk'' without those disadvantages attending upon it. {{right|''Dogs of Great Britain and America'', p. 197.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') A pen in which a gamecock is kept with a certain amount of liberty, but separated from other cocks, to get him in condition and disposition for fighting.}} '''9.''' A district habitually served by a hawker or itinerant vender of any commodity. {{smaller block|One man told me . . . that he had thoughts at one time of trying to establish himself in a cats’-meat ''walk'', and made inquiries into the nature of the calling. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 10.}}}} '''10.''' In the London Royal Exchange, any part of the ambulatory that is specially frequented by merchants or traders to some particular country.   ''Simmonds.''—'''11†.''' A district in a royal forest or park marked out for hunting purposes. {{smaller block|I will keep . . . my shoulders for the fellow of this ''walk'' [''i. e.'', Herne, the hunter, in Windsor Park]. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 29.}}}} {{smaller block|They like better to hunt by stealth in another man’s ''walk''. {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 571.}}}} '''12.''' A ropewalk.—'''13†.''' In ''falconry'', a flock or wisp of snipe.—{{smaller|'''Cock of the walk.''' See ''cock''1.—'''Heel-and-toe walk''', a walk in which the heel of one foot is}}
